study.title: Hosea 12 - Unfaithful covenant, memory of grace and call to return
study.overview: The chapter counters the persistent infidelity of Ephraim and Judah to the faithfulness of God. The people seek security in political alliances, practice deception in trade, pride themselves on their wealth and maintain idolatry, but the Lord recalls his old relationship with Israel, his care throughout history and the means he sent to correct them. The center of the chapter is the call to return to the God of the covenant, practicing mercy and justice, but the continual refusal brings judgment on the guilt and shame of the people.

outline.title: False security and divine contention
outline.explanation: Ephraim runs after empty solutions, making agreements with foreign powers and multiplying lies. The Lord also brings his complaint against Judah and announces retribution according to Jacob's ways, showing that the problem is not only political, but spiritual and moral.

outline.title: Jacob as memory, God as called to repentance
outline.explanation: The memory of Jacob fights in the womb and then with God at Bethel serves as a mirror for Israel: the same God who revealed himself to his parents is the God to whom the people should turn. Therefore the direct exhortation arises: to convert, to keep mercy and righteousness, and to wait continually in God.

outline.title: Religious and material injustice, despite divine provision
outline.explanation: The people are denounced for commercial fraud, self-confidence and self-justification. In contrast, the Lord remembers that he was the one who delivered Israel from Egypt, spoke by prophets, and multiplied visions and parables, that is, there were no warnings or instruction.

outline.title: Idolatry, dependency history and final judgment
outline.explanation: Corruption in places linked to worship shows that external religiosity is also contaminated. Then the story of Jacob and Israel highlights the humility of his origins and the care of God in his preservation, until Ephraim seriously offended the Lord and therefore bear his guilt and shame.

study.context: The chapter dialogues with known episodes of the history of Israel mentioned in the text itself and in the notes: alliances with Assyria and seeking support in Egypt, reference to Bethel, Gilead, Gilgal, Exodus and Jacob's life. The picture is that of a people who have received revelation and direction through the prophets, but has chosen human trust, injustice and idolatry.
study.theology: Hosea 12 presents God as a judge of the covenant and also as the one who calls the return. Divine holiness does not ignore fraud, idolatry, and self-deception; it repays according to the ways. At the same time, Jacob's memory shows that God acts in history with grace and discipline, and the call of verse 6 summarizes the correct answer: conversion, mercy, justice, and perseverance in hope in God. True security comes not from political covenants or wealth, but from obedient communion with the Lord. The text also highlights the sufficiency of the means of revelation: God spoke of prophets, visions and figures, so that disobedience does not occur due to the absence of light, but by resistance of the heart.

scholarViews.insight: The expression about feeding in wind points to empty hopes of human aid; alliances with Assyria and Egypt reveal the political security attempt that ends in frustration.
The chapter gathers accusations against Israel and Judah, especially fraud and injustice, and also the call to return to God; the charge against Ephraim shows that he needed this exhortation.
God spoke of prophets, multiplying visions and using comparisons, symbols, and parables to instruct and save the people; yet they did not take advantage of divine indulgence.

questions: In which areas I, like Ephraim, can I be seeking security in human solutions, rather than continually waiting in God?
Has my practice of faith been accompanied by mercy and justice, or just religious appearance?
What means of correction and instruction has God used in my life, and how have I answered them?
study.practice: Read the chapter as an examination of consciousness: identify false trust, a sin of injustice, and an area of self-justification. Then respond with concrete actions this week: adjust an unfair relationship, reject a dishonest practice, and set aside daily time to turn to the Lord in sincere prayer, asking him to align his heart with mercy, justice and persevering hope.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not unanimously clarify all historical details and some applications vary between commentators. The biblical text cited here already comes with numbering and paraphrasis in Portuguese, and the study follows this basis without resorting to external data not confirmed by the notes. In particular, the reading of certain symbols, such as the return to the tents in verse 9, is presented as an interpretation of the notes, not as an absolute definition of meaning.
